q: Which correctly distinguishes substrate-level phosphorylation from oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Substrate-level moves phosphate from an intermediate to ADP; oxidative uses a proton gradient and ATP synthase
Substrate-level requires O2 as the final electron acceptor; oxidative phosphorylation can occur without any oxygen
Substrate-level occurs only in chloroplasts; oxidative occurs only in the cytoplasm of prokaryotes and eukaryotes
Both use ATP synthase in the inner membrane, but only substrate-level phosphorylation produces any reduced NAD
explanation: In glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, enzymes transfer a phosphate group straight from a phosphorylated substrate to ADP – a small yield (net 2 ATP from glycolysis and 2 from Krebs per glucose). Most ATP (~26–28 per glucose) comes from oxidative phosphorylation: energy from the electron transport chain pumps H+, and H+ flowing back through ATP synthase phosphorylates ADP. Photophosphorylation in chloroplasts also uses chemiosmosis.
